title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 33
paragraphs: When Megabates had taken on the force along with the Naxian exiles, he sailed with the pretense of going to the Hellespont; but when he came to Chios, he directed his ships to Caucasa, to cross over from there to Naxos with a north wind. Then—since it was not fated that the Naxians should be destroyed by this expedition—the following thing happened. As Megabates was going round inspecting the watches set on the several ships, it chanced that on a ship from Myndus no one was on guard; and he, being very angry, ordered his spearmen to find out the captain of that ship, whose name was Scylax, and to bind him in an oar-hole of his ship in such a way that his head should be outside and his body within. When Scylax had been bound in this way, someone reported to Aristagoras that Megabates had bound his guest-friend of Myndus and was treating him with shameful outrage. Aristagoras came and asked the Persian to release him, and when he got nothing of what he was asking for, he went himself and set him free. On hearing this, Megabates was enormously angry and burst out in rage against Aristagoras. Aristagoras replied: “What have you to do with these matters? Did not Artaphrenes send you to obey me and sail wherever I should order? Why do you meddle with things that are not your concern?” So said Aristagoras; and the other, enraged at this, when night came on sent men by ship to Naxos to warn the Naxians of all the danger threatening them.
